text: Chapter two asked whether a series is stationary. Chapter three is about modeling it once it is. Autoregressive, moving average, and their combination, ARMA, are the building blocks that ARIMA and even the GARCH models in chapter four build on.

An AR model says today's value is a weighted sum of its own recent past, plus noise — effects decay gradually and, in principle, never fully disappear. An MA model says today's value depends on recent shocks instead, and those effects cut off sharply after q lags. ARMA combines both in one equation, and often needs fewer total parameters than a pure AR or pure MA model would need on its own.

In statsmodels, you fit ARMA with the ARIMA class and d set to zero — ARIMA with no differencing is exactly ARMA applied to a series that's already stationary. You pass the order as p, d, q, call fit, and read off phi, theta, and the noise variance from the fitted parameters.

Two conditions keep the math well behaved. Stationarity requires the AR side's characteristic roots to sit outside the unit circle — the same unit-root idea from chapter two, now generalized to any number of AR lags. Invertibility requires the same of the MA side's roots, and that's what guarantees a unique set of theta coefficients instead of several different models fitting the data equally well. You rarely check these roots by hand; statsmodels will warn you, or simply fail to converge cleanly, when a fit violates them.

AR captures gradual, momentum-like dependence; MA captures short, sharp shocks; ARMA blends both economically. Next, lesson twelve extends this to non-stationary and seasonal series with ARIMA and SARIMA.
